title: Signs of progress
hookLine: the one making progress blames no one, praises no one, and claims to know nothing (Enchiridion 48)

lines: HOW WOULD YOU KNOW IT'S WORKING?
A CALM MIND HAS NO COUNTER.
cards: How would you know if any of this is working? Progress is easy to count with a language or a marathon: words learned, miles run. A calmer mind doesn't come with a counter.
Epictetus' students wanted to know the same thing: am I actually getting anywhere? Section forty-eight answers them with a checklist, and it isn't the one anyone expects.
Nothing on it about feeling peaceful, or knowing more. It's mostly about what you stop doing.

teach.h: HELP AND HARM COME FROM INSIDE.
teach.b: The ordinary person, Epictetus says, expects help or harm to come from outside. The person on this path expects it from inside, from their own judgments. Then the checklist.

teach.h: BLAMES NO ONE, PRAISES NO ONE.
teach.b: The one making progress blames no one. Praises no one. Finds fault with no one.
Accuses no one. Says nothing about themselves as if they were somebody, or knew something. When blocked, they look to themselves.
When praised, they laugh quietly to themselves at the one praising. When criticized, they don't defend themselves.
Such a person, he says, goes about like someone recovering from an illness, careful not to disturb something that's healing before it has set firm. Progress here isn't a trophy.
It's a mending bone, and you walk carefully on it.
The Stoics called this prokopē, progress, and the one making it a prokoptōn. Epictetus doesn't describe arriving. He describes someone on the road.
You'll never be told you've arrived.
But you can notice, on an ordinary Tuesday, that you didn't blame anyone for the traffic, didn't need the compliment, didn't defend yourself against the remark. Small, quiet, real signs.
And notice which one leads the list. Not courage, not wisdom. Blame no one.

how: People practicing Stoicism sometimes review Epictetus' signs of progress, especially blaming no one, as a quiet self-check at the end of the day.

o: progress: the quiet signs of someone on the road
the calm state of someone who has fully arrived
a Stoic word for patience in suffering

games.q: signs of progress — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus' signs of progress are mostly about feeling calm
they're mostly about what you stop doing: blaming, praising, accusing.
when criticized, the one making progress makes no defense
and when praised, they laugh quietly at the one praising.

games.q: your project fails, partly because of a colleague. what would the one making progress do first?
o: make sure everyone knows whose fault it was.
blame no one, and look to their own part.
say it's fine and praise the colleague.
games.why: the first sign on the list: blames no one. when blocked, the one making progress looks to themselves.

practice: Run Epictetus' checklist slowly, as a mirror, not a test: blames no one, praises no one, finds fault with no one, says nothing about being somebody, laughs a little at praise, doesn't defend against criticism.
Which is closest to true for you lately, and which is farthest? Hold that one gently, like a bone that's still mending.

wordCard.voice: Prokopē. The Stoic word for progress, and the one making it. Its first sign, in Enchiridion forty-eight: blame no one. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: progress. The Stoics called the one making it a prokoptōn.

carryVoice: Your line: blame no one. Help and harm start from inside. Day three hundred eighty-three.
